title: Dhul Hijjah: the best days
hook: extra deeds in the first ten
tomorrow: the pilgrims stand on a plain. what about everyone at home?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shawwal: six fasts after Eid, and one small habit kept. Carry Ramadan forward. Now skip ahead in the year, to ten crowded days.

Exams on Monday. A double shift on Wednesday. A cousin's move on the weekend. Some weeks have no spare inch in them, and the last thing anyone wants is a list of extra things to do. Then the calendar turns to Dhul Hijjah, the month of the Hajj, and its first ten days arrive with a claim attached. The Prophet ﷺ said that no good deeds done on other days are better than those done in these days. His companions were so surprised they asked him a question back.
screen: `A WEEK WITH NO SPARE INCH.` → `DHUL HIJJAH ARRIVES.` → `NO DAYS BETTER FOR GOOD DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Ibn 'Abbas tells it, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The companions asked: not even jihad, striving in God's path? And he said: not even jihad, except a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with none of it. So ordinary deeds in these ten days carry a weight the companions didn't expect. Some commentators hear these days in the Qur'an too, where God swears by the dawn, and, in Pickthall's words, "And ten nights." The pilgrims are in Mecca. But the hadith isn't only about them. It's about anyone, anywhere, doing good in these days. People keep it in small ways: a voluntary fast, the takbir said out loud, God is greater, in the market and at home, a little extra charity, a page more of Qur'an. Here's the part that fits a crammed week. Nothing in the hadith asks for something heroic. It asks for good deeds, the regular kind, done in a season when they count for more. A short dhikr between study blocks. A call to a grandparent on the drive. A few coins in a jar. The ten days don't need an empty calendar. They need small things, more of them.
screen: `NOT EVEN JIHAD?` · `AND TEN NIGHTS.` · `FOR ANYONE, ANYWHERE.` · `SMALL THINGS, MORE OF THEM.` · then, large: `THE BEST TEN.`

segments.voice: On paper, write the numbers one to ten down the side. Next to each, one small extra thing that would fit that day: a coin given, a call to an elder, a short fast, a page. Keep the list in front of you and look it over for the rest of the sit.
screen: `ONE TO TEN, BY HAND.` · `ONE SMALL EXTRA FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: Dhul Hijjah: the month of the Hajj. Its first ten days, the Prophet said, have no equal for good deeds.
The line for today: the best ten, ordinary deeds in a stretch that weighs them more. Small things, done more.

howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many Muslims add voluntary fasts, say the takbir aloud, give extra charity and read more Qur'an, while the pilgrims gather in Mecca for the Hajj.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 969 (Ibn 'Abbas: no good deeds on other days are better than in these; 'not even jihad?')
Sunan Abi Dawud 2438 (the same report, naming 'these ten days')
Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Two Eids, chapter on deeds in the days of tashriq (Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayra saying the takbir in the market in the ten days)

notes: Bukhari 969 (and Abu Dawud 2438 naming the ten days of Dhul Hijjah): confirm; the jihad exception paraphrased as 'goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with none of it'.
Qur'an 89:2: confirm Pickthall's exact wording ('And ten nights'). Reading it as Dhul Hijjah's ten is attributed to 'some commentators' (e.g. Ibn Kathir).

The takbir in the market rests on a mu'allaq report in Bukhari's chapter heading; described as a practice, not a rule. Voluntary fasting in the ten days stated as something people do; no claim the Prophet fasted all nine.
Title 'the best days' and carry 'the best ten' follow the index; the voice ties 'best' to the hadith's own words.
